content: Theanine is an amino acid that is predominantly found in tea, specifically in infusions made from the leaves of Camellia sinensis. Structurally, theanine is closely related to glutamine and has the ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. Due to its capacity to enter the brain, theanine exhibits psychoactive properties. Theanine has been demonstrated to reduce both mental and physical stress, and it may induce a state of relaxation. It is hypothesized that these effects are mediated through an increase in the production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter that plays a key role in promoting calmness and reducing neuronal excitability. Additionally, theanine has been shown to elevate levels of serotonin, dopamine, and GABA in the brain. It also exhibits micromolar binding affinities for AMPA, kainate, and NMDA receptors, which are critical components of the glutamatergic system. In animal studies, such as those involving spontaneously hypertensive mice, theanine administration has been associated with a significant reduction in brain levels of 5-hydroxyindole, a metabolite of serotonin. Researchers have also proposed that theanine may inhibit glutamic acid excitotoxicity, a pathological process that can lead to neuronal damage or death due to excessive stimulation by glutamate. Theanine has been found to promote the production of alpha brain waves, which are associated with a relaxed yet alert mental state. Experimental studies in rats have shown that even when administered in extremely high doses repeatedly, theanine produces minimal to no adverse psychological or physical effects, indicating a high safety profile. L-theanine may also enhance the immune system's ability to combat infections. It has been shown to boost the activity of gamma delta T cells, a subset of immune cells that play a role in the body's defense against pathogens. A study conducted in 2003 by Brigham and Women's Hospital involved a four-week trial with 11 coffee drinkers and 10 tea drinkers, each consuming 600 milliliters of coffee or black tea daily. Analysis of blood samples revealed that tea drinkers exhibited up to a fivefold increase in the production of anti-bacterial proteins, suggesting a stronger immune response compared to coffee drinkers. In recent years, tea companies have highlighted the natural presence of L-theanine in their products, emphasizing its ability to enhance alpha brainwave production and its potential health benefits.
